1. The Accidental Release Prevention Program
ChampionX is committed to being a responsible member of the community in which it operates  by giving top priority to operating in a safe and environmentally sound manner. The three core policies, safety, environmental, and sustainability, all state the Company's commitment to providing the resources, processes, facilities, standard training, discipline and work culture to ensure a safe work environment for all employees, safety for the communities in which we operate and safe competitive products for our customers. ChampionX, a Business line of SLB, now known at Production Chemical Technologies employees are committed to being supportive members of the communities in which we operate by integrating economic, social, and environmental considerations into day to day business and long range planning. 

The Accidental Release Prevention Programs at the Plant include daily toolbox meetings, a weekly safety meeting for all employees, and a weekly meeting of the safety advocates with representation from each department. The Plant has an onsite Emergency Response Team (ERT) with representation from each shift in order to engage the system 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. 

2. Site sources and regulated substances
The stationary sources and regulated substances handled at the ChampionX Sugar Land Plant is a chemical manufacturing plant located at 7701 Highway 90 Alternate, Sugar Land, Texas. The manufacturing plant is a batch chemical processing facility which produces industrial organic chemicals used primarily in the oil and gas industry exploration and production industry. The plant is staffed 24 hours a day, 7 days a week year-round and has full-time security personnel. There are four RMP-regulated materials and associated processes at the facility: 
	Epichlorohydrin (106-89-8) 
	Ethylenediamine (107-15-3)
	Ammonia Solution (7664-41-7)
	Formaldehyde Solution (50-00-0) 
Note: As of January 1, 2025 the Plant no longer exc

eeds the threshold quantity for Vinyl Acetate and Cyclohexylamine.   Historically, both of these materials were stored in aboveground storage tanks.  Both tanks have been cleaned out andisolated from the process.  Both chemicals are now managed in smaller packages with an inventory well below the threshold quantity.

The plant uses these regulated substances and other raw organic and inorganic materials to create products used in multiple applications in the oil and gas industry. The bulk of materials produced at the Sugar Land Plant are either oil-soluble or water-soluble intermediates and products. Raw materials are received by rail car, bulk cargo tank truck, and in drums and totes. Finished products are shipped via rail car, bulk cargo tank truck, and in box trucks for drums and totes. The remaining raw materials other than the four RMP-covered chemicals are either not RMP-regulated substances or not present in the processes in quantities that trigger RMP applicability.

3.  Hazard Assessment for the process
A Hazard Assessment was completed consistent with the 40 CFR 68, Subpart B
Requirements and EPAs Offsite Consequence Analysis (OCA) guidance. The worst-case release scenario(s) and the alternative release scenario(s), including Passive (administrative controls) and Active mitigation measures were considered per §68.25 and §68.28  to limit the impact distances under each reported scenario.  RMPComp was used for modeling worst case and alternative release scenarios. 

4. General Accidental Release Prevention Program and chemical-specific prevention steps.
The following is a summary of the general accident prevention program in place at the Sugar Land Plant facility. Processes at the facility are regulated by both the EPA RMP regulation and the OSHA PSM standard. The plant RMP/PSM programs incorporate all of the RMP/PSM elements identified in the regulations.

4.1 Employee Participation [29 CFR §1910.119(c)]
The Sugar Land Plant encourages employees to partici

pate in all facets of risk management and
accident prevention. Examples of employee participation include updating and compiling
procedures, participating as members of audit teams, participating as members of a Process Hazard
Analysis (PHA) team, incident investigations/corrective actions, plant safety advocates, and daily safety briefings / toolbox meetings.  Employees have access to all information created either by hardcopy or electronically on the Companys SharePoint site. A culture that drives towards zero accidents and incidents is the focus of ChampionXs Safety, Health, and Environment Policies.  In addition, the Sugar Land Plant has a number of initiatives that address process failures, process safety education and employee safety issues. These initiatives include forming teams including: HAZOPS, Process Improvement, andSafety Advocate Teams. In addition, a hazard reporting system is in place to identify, report, and track employee reports on near misses. Each near miss is discussed in the morning meeting Monday - Friday with corrective actions assigned and documented in the system.

4.2 Process Safety Information (PSI) 29 CFR §1910.119(d)]
The Sugar Land Plant keeps a variety of technical documents and standard operating procedures that are used to help maintain safe operation of the processes. These documents address chemical properties and associated hazards, limits for key process parameters and specific chemical   inventories, as well as  equipment design basis/configuration information. Specific departments within the facility are assigned responsibility for maintaining up-to-date process safety information.  

Chemical-specific information, including exposure hazards and emergency response/exposure treatment considerations, is provided in safety data sheets (SDSs). This information addresses any known hazards associated with the use and handling of chemicals. The facility ensures that processes are maintained within operating limits using process c

ontrols, monitoring instruments, and highly trained personnel. The facility also maintains numerous technical documents that provide information about the design and construction of process equipment. This information includes materials of construction, design pressures, temperature ratings and electrical ratings of equipment, etc. This information, in combination with written operational procedures and trained personnel, provides a basis for inspection and maintenance activities, as well as for evaluating proposed process and facility changes to ensure that safety features in each process are not compromised.

4.3 Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) [29 CFR §1910.119(e)]
The Sugar Land Plant has a comprehensive program to help ensure that hazards associated with the
various processes are identified and controlled. Within this program, each process is systematically
examined to identify hazards and ensure that adequate controls are in place to manage these
hazards. The Sugar Land Plant predominately uses the Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP)
technique to perform Process Hazard Analysis (PHA). The analyses are conducted using a team of
people who have operating and maintenance experience as well as engineering expertise. This
team identifies and evaluates hazards of the process as well as accident prevention and mitigation
measures, and makes suggestions for additional prevention and/or mitigation measures when the
team believes such measures are necessary.

The PHA team findings are forwarded to management for review. Implementation of mitigation
options in response to PHA findings are based on a relative risk ranking assigned by the PHA team.
This ranking helps ensure that potential accident scenarios assigned the highest risk receive
attention first. All approved mitigation options being implemented in response to PHA team findings
are tracked to completion. The final resolution of each finding is documented and retained.  

To help ensure that the process controls a

nd/or process hazards do not eventually deviate
significantly from the original design safety features, the Sugar Land Plant periodically updates and
revalidates the hazard analysis results. These periodic reviews are conducted at least every 5 years
and will be conducted at this frequency until the process is no longer operating. The results and
findings from these updates are documented and retained. Once again, the team findings are
forwarded to management for consideration and the final resolution of the findings is documented
and retained.

4.4 Operating Procedures 29 CFR §1910.119(f)]
The Sugar Land Plant maintains written procedures that address various modes of process operations,
such as (1) unit startup, (2) normal operations, (3) temporary operations, (4) emergency shutdown,
(5) normal shutdown, and (6) initial startup of a new process. The procedures clearly state operating
limits, consequences for deviation, and appropriate responses for deviation. These procedures can
be used as a reference by experienced operators and provide a basis for consistent training of new
operators. The procedures are maintained current and accurate by revising them as necessary.
These procedures are reviewed and certified annually as current and accurate. The operating
procedures are available in the company intranet (Intelex).  

4.5 Training [29 CFR §1910.119(g)]
To complement the written procedures for process operations, the Sugar Land Plant has implemented a comprehensive training program for all employees involved in operating a regulated process. New employees receive basic training in facility operations. After successfully completing this training, a new operator is paired with the Plant Trainer (position is filled by an experienced operator from production) to learn process-specific duties and tasks. Operators must demonstrate (e.g., through tests, skills demonstration) having adequate knowledge to perform the duties and tasks in a safe manner on their own before t

hey can work independently. In addition, all operators periodically receive refresher training on the operating procedures to ensure that their skills and knowledge are maintained at a competent level. All of this training is documented for each operator, including the means used to verify that the operator understood the training. Initial and refresher training records are retained and reviewed periodically.  



4.6 Contractors [29 CFR §1910.119(h)]
The Sugar Land Plant uses contractors to supplement its workforce for some maintenance specialties, construction activities, and forklift operators. Because some contractors work on or near process equipment, the facility has procedures in place to ensure that contractors receive training before beginning work on or near a covered process. Training consists of completing Safety Essentials and a Site Specific Training administered by the Houston Area Safety Council.  Training is also provided by the contractors lead and site coordinator to ensure all contractors:
	Can perform their work in a safe manner, 
	Have the appropriate knowledge and skills, 
	Are aware of the hazards in their workplace, 
	Understand what they should do in the event of an emergency,
	Understand and follow site safety rules, and 
	Can inform facility personnel of any hazards that they find during their work.
This is accomplished by providing contractors with (1) a process overview, (2) information about safety and health hazards, (3) emergency response plan requirements, and (4) safe work practices prior to their beginning work. In addition, contractors are evaluated with respect to their existing programs and performance during the selection of a contractor. High risk contractors are periodically monitored to ensure that they are fulfilling their safety obligations. 

4.7 Pre-startup Safety Reviews (PSSRs) [29 CFR §1910.119(i)]
The Sugar Land Plant conducts a PSSR for any new plant modification that requires a change in the process safety

information. The purpose of the PSSR is to ensure that safety features, procedures, personnel, and the equipment are appropriately prepared for startup prior to placing the equipment into service. This review provides an additional check to make sure construction is in accordance with the design specifications and that all supporting systems are operationally ready. The PSSR review team uses checklists to verify all aspects of readiness. A PSSR involves field verification of the construction and serves a quality assurance function by requiring verification that accident prevention program requirements are properly implemented.  

4.8 Mechanical Integrity [29 CFR §1910.119(j)]
The Sugar Land Plant has well-established practices and procedures in place to maintain pressure vessels, piping systems, relief and vent systems, controls, pumps and compressors, and emergency shutdown systems in a safe operating condition. The basic aspects of this program include: 
	Conducting training, 
	Developing written procedures, 
	Performing inspections and tests, 
	Correcting identified deficiencies, and 
	applying quality assurance measures. 

In combination, these activities form a program that maintains the mechanical integrity of the process equipment.  Another integral part of the mechanical integrity program is quality assurance. The Sugar Land Plant incorporates quality assurance measures into equipment purchases and repairs. This helps ensure that new equipment is suitable for its intended use and that proper material and spare parts are used when repairs are made. Inspections and tests are performed to help ensure that equipment functions as intended, and to verify that equipment is maintained within acceptable limits (e.g., adequate wall thickness for pressure vessels). Inspections and tests are conducted per manufacturer recommendations or industry standards. If a deficiency is identified, employees will correct the deficiency before placing the equipment back into se

rvice (if possible), or a Management of Change (MOC) team will review the use of the equipment and determine what actions are necessary to ensure the safe operation of the equipment. Inspection/test records are retained per §68.73(d).


4.9 Safe Work Practices [29 CFR §1910.119(k)]
The Sugar Land Plant has four core safe work permit practices in place to help ensure worker and process safety. The four permit practices include: 
1.	General Permit to control the entry/presence/exit of support personnel, 
2.	Lockout/tagout procedure/permit (LOTO) to ensure isolation of energy sources for equipment undergoing maintenance which also includes reference to the line break procedure for safe removal of hazardous materials before process piping or equipment is opened 
3.	Hot Work procedure/permit to control spark-producing activities (i.e., hot work)
4.	Confined Space permit and procedure to ensure that adequate precautions are in place before entry into a confined space. 

These procedures (and others), along with training of affected personnel, form a system to help ensure that operations and maintenance activities are performed safely.  Permits are reviewed and updated periodically.

4.10 Management of Change [29 CFR §1910.119(l)]
The Sugar Land Plant has a system to manage changes to processes. This system requires that changes to items such as process equipment, chemicals, technology (including process-operating
conditions), procedures, and other facility changes be properly reviewed and authorized before implementation. Changes are reviewed prior to implementation to:
	Ensure that adequate controls are in place to manage any new hazards 
	Verify that existing controls have not been compromised by the change.
	Minimize or eliminate impact on safety and health

Affected chemical hazard information, process operating limits, equipment information, and procedures are updated to incorporate these changes. In addition, operating and maintenance personnel are provided any n

ecessary training on the change.  Documentation is retained for all MOCs and integrated into PHA reviews.  

4.11 Incident Investigation [29 CFR §1910.119(m)]
The Sugar Land Plant promptly investigates all incidents that resulted in or reasonably could have resulted in a fire/explosion or toxic gas release that could lead to personal injury, severe environmental impact, or major property damage. The goal of each investigation is to determine the facts and develop corrective actions to prevent a recurrence of the incident or a similar incident. The investigation team documents its findings, develops recommendations to prevent a recurrence, and forwards these results to facility management for resolution. Corrective actions taken in response to the investigation team's findings and recommendations are tracked until they are complete. The final resolution of each finding or recommendation is documented, and the investigation results are reviewed with all employees (including contractors) who could be affected by the findings. Incident investigation reports are retained for at least 5 years so that the reports can be reviewed during future PHAs and PHA revalidations.

4.12 Compliance Audits  [29 CFR §1910.119(o)]
To help ensure that the accident prevention program is functioning properly, the Sugar Land Plant facility periodically conducts an audit to determine whether the procedures and practices required by the accident prevention program are being implemented. Compliance audits are conducted annually and focus on a subset of the required compliance topics with all topics covered at least once every 3 years.  Both hourly and management personnel participate as audit team members. The audit team develops findings that are forwarded to facility management for resolution. Corrective actions taken in response to the audit team's findings are tracked until they are complete. The final resolution of each finding is documented, and the two most recent audit reports are retai

ned.  

5. The five-year accident history
No accidents meeting the criteria of §68.42(a) have occurred at the Sugar Land Plant in the past five years.

6. The emergency response program
ChampionX has implemented a written Emergency Response Program Plan to prepare for andrespond to accidental releases of hazardous materials, fires, natural disasters, and/or acts of terrorism. The plan includes; 
	All aspects of emergency response from initial discovery
	Defensive response actions that can reduce the severity/extent of the spill/release if can be done without risking injury or exposure to personnel
	Response to spills/releases, plant alarms, emergency reporting, and evaluation/ accountability 
	Procedures for notification of emergency responders and public agencies

A draft organizational chart and key Incident Command System (ICS) forms are also included in the EAP. Employees receive annual training in emergency procedures. 

In addition, all operations employees attend Hazwoper training which includes both a field exercise where each employee extinguishes a live fire and either classroom or computer-based training.  Annual emergency response training including hazardous substance release scenarios is covered during annual Hazwoper training.  To ensure proper functioning, emergency response equipment is regularly inspected, serviced, and results / actions are documented.  In addition, the plan is promptly updated to reflect any pertinent changes taking place within processes that would require a modified emergency response.

The Plant has an onsite Emergency Response Team that is manned for all shifts and provides coverage to the Plant 24/7.  The ERT is part of the Plants Emergency Response Program.  The ERT meets monthly to learn and refresh on topics which involve engaging the following equipment and/or actions:
	Operating and use of fire monitors
	Connecting fire monitors to foam
	Live fire fighting (performed offsite a local fire field)
	Operation of th

e fire panels
	Deluge and foam systems
	First Aid/CPR
	Hazardous Materials response
	Tabletop drills

As part of the annual Hazwoper training, all operations employees demonstrate how to to use a fire extinguisher to put out a live fire. ChampionX provides a safety and environmental handbook for all new hires which covers general safety and environmental best practices. In addition, the Sugar Land Plant participates with the Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC) and has a monthly meeting with the Community Action Committee (CAP) with members from the local community.  

7. Planned changes to improve safety
Studies associated with prevention program elements such as PHAs, incident investigation, management of change, and compliance audits are regularly conducted at the Sugar Land Plant to verify
Design criteria and to identify potential hazards. Recommendations may be developed as a result of these
studies and as a result of equipment inspections, safety meetings, review of industry experience,
technology improvements, and employee suggestions. Once formulated, recommendations are
reviewed, corresponding action items are developed to implement each recommendation, and then
tracked to completion.

The ChampionX Sugar Land Plant is actively working to decrease potential exposure to the community as part of the continuous improvement process.  Within the next two years, Sugar Land Plant anticipates the following changes:
	Epichlorohydrin existing 14,500 gallon tank will be decommissioned and replaced with a 4,000 gallon tank with engineering controls to ensure volume stays below the threshold limit.
	Ethylenediamine will switch from drop trailers to live offload of trailers direct to the process to reduce onsite storage. 
	All products containing 26% aqua ammonia will be reformulated for the raw material to require 19% ammonia.
	All products containing formaldehyde solution will be reformulated for the raw material to require paraformaldehyde.
